**Question:** If two different names in the tree are two names for the very same file on disk (a hard link — for example `notes.txt` and `backup/notes.txt` sharing one inode), should `create` store each name as an ordinary file with its own copy of the contents, or treat the second name as a "hard link" and leave it out? (FR-015 / FR-020)

**Why it matters:** FR-015 currently lists hard links among the things `create` must skip, but on disk a second name for a file is indistinguishable from any other ordinary file — so reading FR-015 literally would silently drop one of the user's files from the archive, and `extract` would rebuild an incomplete tree.

**Recommended:** Option A - Hard-linkedness isn't a property of a file you can see by looking at it; it only becomes a distinct member type when an archiver chooses to record it that way. Storing each name as the ordinary file it is keeps the guarantee that every regular file beneath a named path appears in the archive (SC-001) and keeps `create`/`extract` round-trips complete. The cost is duplicated bytes in the rare tree that uses hard links, which is a far better outcome than a missing file.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Each name is stored as an independent regular file with its own contents and counted separately. FR-015's mention of hard links is corrected to apply only to reading existing archives, where the member type genuinely exists. |
| B | Keep FR-015 literal: notice when a name points at a file already added, skip it, name it on standard error, and don't count it. The archive then holds the contents once under one name only. |
| C | Store the second name as a tar hard-link member pointing at the first, so the bytes aren't duplicated. `extract` would then skip it as a non-regular member, so the extracted tree is missing that name. |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (≤5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
